scholarly_argument_donini_aristotle_s_pr.pdf_source: [local-path] SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/01_Philosophie_antique/ Pier Luigi Donini - Aristotle and Determinism (2010, Peeters) - libgen.li.pdf
scholarly_argument_donini_aristotle_s_pr.chapter: Ch. I — Words and Things, Truth and Facts (opening)
scholarly_argument_donini_aristotle_s_pr.quote_verbatim: Toward the end of chapter 9 of de Interpretatione, at 19a33, Aristotle introduces his famous solution to the problem of future-tense singular propositions by invoking a general principle of his philosophy: 'since statements are true in the same way as facts' — where the Greek nouns placed in relation to truth are logoi and pragmata. […] there is no doubt that it does indeed represent a position consistently held by Aristotle in his works, where one finds even the further specification that truth, as conformity of logoi to pragmata, ultimately implies a causal dependence of the former from the latter: on this thesis the Categories agree with the middle books of the Metaphysics. It is therefore a general and important principle, and not only for Aristotle's logic: it is ultimately the only criterion for truth that Aristotle recognizes.
scholarly_argument_donini_aristotle_s_pr.context: Direct attestation of the correspondence principle (logoi to pragmata) thesis: position consistently held, causal dependence of statements on extralinguistic reality, only criterion for truth Aristotle recognizes. Donini sets it out in the opening 2pp. of Ch. I (the chapter on de Interpretatione 9) so that the principle can then be used as the diagnostic criterion for unmasking the deterministic argument's flaw later in the chapter. Footnote refs.: Hadot 319; Cat. 14b15-23; Metaph. IX 1051b3-9; Viano 28.

scholarly_argument_donini_status_of_futu.pdf_source: [local-path] SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/01_Philosophie_antique/ Pier Luigi Donini - Aristotle and Determinism (2010, Peeters) - libgen.li.pdf
scholarly_argument_donini_status_of_futu.chapter: Ch. I — Words and Things, Truth and Facts §1
scholarly_argument_donini_status_of_futu.quote_verbatim: But what is the precise function of this principle in the solution of a question such as that of future contingents, where the possibility of the conformity of logoi to pragmata immediately presents itself as, to say the least, problematic? In what sense is the future, or a future state of affairs, presented by Aristotle as a pragma, or in what sense might it be? And if the future is not, and is not thought by Aristotle to be, in some way, a pragma, would there be any point then in referring to the principle of the conformity of logoi to pragmata if not simply to exclude the possibility of speaking of truth for the future? According to a respectable number of ancient and modern commentators, however, Aristotle does not exclude that it is possible, in some fashion, to speak of truth also for logoi concerning the future; and certainly it seems difficult and inadvisable to interpret the conclusion of de Int. 9 in a such a way as to find in it a categorical and absolute prohibition against speaking of truth also for the future.
scholarly_argument_donini_status_of_futu.context: Donini's thesis that the future-as-pragma is problematic but that Aristotle restricts rather than abolishes truth-for-the-future. The KG description's 'ouk homoiōs, not oudamēs' is supported in Donini's own footnote 7 (p.3): 'οὐχ ὁμοίως, 18a34. One can easily see that this wording is not at all equivalent to οὐδαμῶς; what is suggested from the outset is that we think of a restriction, not of the abolition of the logical principle under discussion.'

scholarly_argument_donini_aristotle_s_re.pdf_source: [local-path] SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/01_Philosophie_antique/ Pier Luigi Donini - Aristotle and Determinism (2010, Peeters) - libgen.li.pdf
scholarly_argument_donini_aristotle_s_re.chapter: Ch. I — Words and Things, Truth and Facts §2
scholarly_argument_donini_aristotle_s_re.quote_verbatim: Having recognized this, it is not difficult to uncover the (nearly) perfect parallel between the deterministic argument in II and Aristotle's counter-argument in III: from the wholesale application (let us call it premise a) of the logical principle to the future as well, the determinist would derive (b), the necessity of everything that happens; from here one would further deduce (c, at 18b31) the futility of deliberation and of any human initiative. Aristotle responds in section III by first of all denying c (19a8), and certainly also by broadening the discussion (we will see later how and why); having denied c, he can then return to thesis b, from which the deterministic argument would have derived c, and deny that too, establishing thus that, factually, not everything happens by necessity (19a18-32). He feels authorized at that point (19a32-33) to move backward from facts to logoi and finally denies the wholesale validity of the logical principle asserted by the determinists in a. More schematically: Section II (deterministic argument) if a given principle a is valid then all happens by necessity (b) and one can deduce from this that it is futile to deliberate (c) | Section III (Aristotle's reply) but c is not true therefore it is manifest that b is not true either therefore principle a ought not to be valid (it must be qualified)
scholarly_argument_donini_aristotle_s_re.context: Direct attestation of the parallel-structure thesis. Donini's reconstruction of Aristotle's c→b→a denial order in de Int. 9 III matches the KG description verbatim (premises a, b, c labelling and the order: deny c first, then b, finally a). Donini's diagnosis of the deterministic argument's 'fundamental flaw' as a violation of the correspondence principle is set out two paragraphs earlier (p.3): 'instead of moving from things to establish the truth of statements, the argument assumes as universally valid a principle regarding logoi and from there claims to draw conclusions about how things are.'

scholarly_argument_donini_nicomachean_et.pdf_source: [local-path] SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/01_Philosophie_antique/ Pier Luigi Donini - Aristotle and Determinism (2010, Peeters) - libgen.li.pdf
scholarly_argument_donini_nicomachean_et.chapter: Ch. IV — Character and Indeterminacy §6 (with Ch. VI — Voluntariness of Vice and Virtue, NE III 1-5, p. 137ff., as parallel locus)
scholarly_argument_donini_nicomachean_et.quote_verbatim: An entirely different and far more troubling point, however, could be what Aristotle says in NE III 5, 1113b7-14: 'in cases where acting depends on us, not acting also depends on us, and, conversely, where the no, also the yes; so that, if it depends on us to act when the action is fine, it will also depend on us not to act when not acting is shameful; and if it depends on us not to act when not acting is fine, it will also depend on us to act when the action is shameful. If it depends on us to perform fine and shameful actions, and likewise not to perform them and this was, in our view, to be good or bad, then it depends on us to be worthy or vicious people.' Here Aristotle seems to be implying something more than the mere possibility of not taking action; he seems to be saying that, in situations where agents are to perform actions that are 'in their power,' they always have two possible options: of doing (or not doing) good in order not to do (or to do) evil.
scholarly_argument_donini_nicomachean_et.context: The KG description of this argument (which paraphrases Huby's review summary) attributes to Donini the claim that 'at NE 3.5 1113b7-14 Aristotle is concerned with whether virtue and vice are voluntary, producing arguments aimed at showing that they are indeed voluntary; it would be inappropriate at this point to add qualifications about human psychology.' This is Huby's gloss, NOT what Donini himself says. Donini's own treatment is more nuanced: he reads 1113b7-14 as a 'far more troubling point' that creates real tension with the theory of unidirectionality of habits, not as a passage that should be sealed off from psychological complications. The proper locus for the full discussion is Ch. VI (= the translation of 'Volontarietà di vizio e virtù', 1989), which opens (p.137): 'By "voluntariness" of vice and virtue, I mean to refer to Aristotle's assertion at the beginning (1113b6: virtue and vice are eph' hemin) and at the conclusion (1114b19ff. and 22-24: virtue and vice are hekousioi) of chapter 5 of book III of the Nicomachean Ethics.' Recommend: rewrite the KG argument description to match Donini's actual position rather than Huby's compressed restatement.
scholarly_argument_donini_nicomachean_et.description_revision_recommended: Current description is Huby 1991's compressed summary, not Donini's position. Donini does not say it is 'inappropriate to add qualifications about human psychology' — on the contrary, he insists (Ch. IV §6, p.103-104) that 1113b7-14 raises a 'far more troubling' tension with the theory of unidirectionality of habits, which he attempts to resolve in Ch. VI §§1-7. Suggested revised description: 'Donini holds that NE III 5, 1113b7-14, which seems to assert two-way power (the agent can equally do or not-do), creates a real and far-from-trivial tension with Aristotle's general theory of unidirectionality of acquired habits in NE III; resolving this is the central interpretative task of Ch. VI of Ethos 1989 / Ch. VI of Aristotle and Determinism 2010.'

scholarly_argument_donini_the_voluntary_.pdf_source: [local-path] SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/01_Philosophie_antique/ Pier Luigi Donini - Aristotle and Determinism (2010, Peeters) - libgen.li.pdf
scholarly_argument_donini_the_voluntary_.chapter: Ch. V — Natural Endowments §6 (closing argument of the original 1989 Italian Ch. V)
scholarly_argument_donini_the_voluntary_.quote_verbatim: It is warranted, in the first place, because Aristotle does not conceive of the subjects of the Ethics and of the Politics — the men in whose power virtue (or vice) is said to lie — as of individuals who have to solve, each on his own, the problem of choosing between good and evil. It is too often forgotten that these are citizens belonging from birth to a wealthy and educated class […]. It is for this basic reason, perhaps, that one can justifiably say that virtue and vice 'depend on us' — where the plural (eph' hemin) should be considered neither accidental nor irrelevant. No one is left by nature to decide in favor of virtue or vice on their own; all are born within a family and a city which, at least in theory, make available to each individual the basic resources for achieving moral excellence. Thus virtue most certainly does depend on us: on the members of a family and city community naturally oriented towards the goal of fully achieving excellence […] It is clear that in this picture nature, institutions, society, family, education, far from being limits that potentially restrict the 'voluntariness' of virtue and vice, or their 'being in us, depending from us,' are instead the necessary conditions for their unfolding; one can intuitively grasp that such a view would still have been tenable in the late 4th century and that it became difficult to grasp and to adopt immediately, or soon, after. It is evident, finally, that it would be unwise to require Aristotle to solve our own problems regarding freedom of the will, of choice, or of conscience: he spoke of other matters.
scholarly_argument_donini_the_voluntary_.context: Direct verbatim attestation of the plural-eph'hemin thesis. The KG description (originally extracted from Huby's review) is a faithful summary of this very paragraph: Donini takes the plural of eph' hemin seriously, grounds it in citizenship and education in a polis-community, and warns explicitly against reading modern free-will problems back into Aristotle ('he spoke of other matters'). Page 131-132 is the closing argument of the original 1989 Ch. V (Natural Endowments) before the appended essays.

scholarly_argument_donini_aristotle_s_co.pdf_source: [local-path] SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/01_Philosophie_antique/ Pier Luigi Donini - Aristotle and Determinism (2010, Peeters) - libgen.li.pdf
scholarly_argument_donini_aristotle_s_co.page: v (Prefatory Note) + 1 (Ch. I opening) + 79 (Ch. IV opening)
scholarly_argument_donini_aristotle_s_co.chapter: Volume-wide thesis attested in Prefatory Note (p.v), Ch. I opening (p.1), and Ch. IV opening (p.79)
scholarly_argument_donini_aristotle_s_co.quote_verbatim: [Prefatory Note, p.v]: 'This volume provides a translation of the first five chapters of the original Italian edition of my study, Ethos: Aristotele e il determinismo, Alessandria, Edizioni dell'Orso 1989. Also included in the volume are three essays on topics closely related to the problems raised in the chapters of the book, of which the essays can be considered an extension and further development.' [Ch. I, p.1]: 'there is no doubt that it does indeed represent a position consistently held by Aristotle in his works […]. It is therefore a general and important principle, and not only for Aristotle's logic: it is ultimately the only criterion for truth that Aristotle recognizes.' [Ch. III, p.51 / cf. line 2090, p.50ff.]: 'Aristotle is fairly consistent in his presentation of the two groups of events that either never admit variations, or have only a low frequency of variation […].'
scholarly_argument_donini_aristotle_s_co.context: The strong form of this thesis ('Aristotle held a consistent theory or set of theories about determinism, the voluntary, and related matters throughout his life; many misunderstandings have obscured this consistency') is Huby's 1991 Classical Review summary (CR 41/2, p.370): 'his central theme is not entirely clear, but he seems to believe that Aristotle held a consistent theory, or set of theories, about these matters throughout his life. Working on various levels, he tries to show that there have been many misunderstandings which, if corrected, allow us to see Aristotle's thought clearly.' Donini himself does not use such a programmatic formulation in the 2010 Peeters volume; the closest Donini-side textual support is (a) the Prefatory Note's framing of the eight chapters as a unified development, (b) the Ch. I claim that the correspondence principle is 'consistently held by Aristotle in his works' from Categories to Metaphysics IX, and (c) the Ch. III remark that 'Aristotle is fairly consistent' on statistical classes of events. The omitted Ch. VI of the 1989 Italian edition (on Cicero) — which is NOT in the 2010 volume — was reportedly where the consistency-thesis was most explicitly programmatic, but that chapter is not on disk.
scholarly_argument_donini_aristotle_s_co.primary_attestation: Huby 1991 review (paraphrase of Donini 1989); local PDF of 1989 monograph itself not available
scholarly_argument_donini_aristotle_s_co.donini_direct_partial_attestation: Donini 2010, p.v (Prefatory Note), p.1 (Ch. I), p.50ff. (Ch. III)

scholarly_argument_donini_relation_betwe.chapter: Huby's review of Donini 1989, The Classical Review 41/2 (1991), pp.370-371
scholarly_argument_donini_relation_betwe.quote_verbatim: Practically no modern scholar has taken account of both the De interpretatione and the Ethics passages together. D. succeeds in relating them to some extent, but it might be replied that they are concerned with very different matters, the one a logico-epistemological puzzle, the other something approaching the cluster of problems about freewill and determinism which still keeps philosophers busy.
scholarly_argument_donini_relation_betwe.context: This thesis is reported by Huby in her 1991 review (p.370). It corresponds to Donini's strategy in Ethos 1989 of treating de Int. 9 (Chs. I-III of Ethos = Chs. I-III of Aristotle and Determinism 2010) and NE III 1-5 (Ch. VI of 1989 = Ch. VI of 2010) within one volume. In the 2010 Peeters volume, the cross-reference is made implicitly via the volume's architecture (de Int. 9 chapters precede the NE III chapters; both treat 'depending on us' / contingency) but Donini does not assert in just these words that the two passages 'concern different matters, one a logico-epistemological puzzle, the other approaches problems about free will and determinism.' The 1989 monograph itself, where the comparison may have been more explicit, is NOT on disk.
scholarly_argument_donini_relation_betwe.note: Phrasing of the KG description is essentially Huby's, not Donini's own. The thesis is structurally compatible with Donini 2010 (which juxtaposes de Int. 9 and NE III in successive chapters and is keen, in the Prefatory Note, to emphasize that the eight chapters address related but distinct problems) but cannot be verified verbatim from the local 2010 PDF.

scholarly_argument_donini_de_interpretat.chapter: Huby's review of Donini 1989, The Classical Review 41/2 (1991), pp.370-371
scholarly_argument_donini_de_interpretat.quote_verbatim: On a different level he argues, with due caution, that the example of the sea-battle may have been chosen because, until 1918, it was a very chancy matter for two fleets actually to come into contact and so for one side to decide to engage in a battle.
scholarly_argument_donini_de_interpretat.context: This historically pungent remark — that the sea-battle (de Int. 9, 19a30) was chosen by Aristotle as an emblematic chancy event because, in pre-radar / pre-aerial-reconnaissance naval warfare (the limit Huby gives is 1918, the year of the WWI armistice and of the last fully visual naval engagements), it was genuinely contingent whether two fleets at sea would actually find each other and engage — is attested only in Huby's 1991 review. It is NOT in the 2010 Peeters volume: the sea-battle is discussed at p.74ff., p.78, p.79-80 (Ch. IV §1) as the paradigm example of a hopoter' etyche event, but Donini in the 2010 text does not adduce the historical 1918 cut-off argument. The remark must have appeared in the 1989 Italian monograph Ethos (most plausibly in its Ch. III or Ch. IV); that monograph is NOT on disk in DOCTORAT (the file 'aristotle-and-determinism-...1989...pdf' is the Huby review, not the monograph). Direct verification of the 1918 remark requires obtaining a physical or scanned copy of Ethos 1989.
scholarly_argument_donini_de_interpretat.primary_attestation: Huby 1991 review p.370 (paraphrase of Donini 1989); thesis NOT present in Donini 2010
scholarly_argument_donini_de_interpretat.not_in_local_corpus: Donini, Ethos: Aristotele e il determinismo, Alessandria: Edizioni dell'Orso, 1989, vi+154pp. — physical monograph required for direct verification of 1918 sea-battle remark

scholarly_argument_donini_cicero_s_de_fa.chapter: Huby's review of Donini 1989, The Classical Review 41/2 (1991), pp.370-371
scholarly_argument_donini_cicero_s_de_fa.quote_verbatim: Finally D. considers Cicero's De Fato, which lists Aristotle with Democritus, Heraclitus and Empedocles as ones who held omnia ita fato fieri, ut id fatum vim necessitatis adferret. Cicero's sources are still disputed, but D. argues strongly that we must forget Antiochus and think rather of Carneades via Clitomachus, although possibly Cicero might have added Aristotle's name independently of his main source. Aristotle is placed in this group because Cicero thinks that in his view the movements of the soul, which are at the centre of the discussion, are caused by external forces, which amount to Fate. External circumstances, such as climate, or natural endowments, have their effect on men's behaviour, and it is said in the Magna Moralia (1187b29), possibly known at this time, that nature (phusis) is needed for a man to be good. Perhaps this was the line of thought.
scholarly_argument_donini_cicero_s_de_fa.context: Huby reports Donini's central argument in Ch. VI of Ethos 1989: Cicero's grouping of Aristotle with Democritus, Heraclitus, Empedocles as determinists (Cic. De Fato, fr. preserved in Aug. CD V 9 = Cic. Fat. fr.1 Sharples?) should be traced to Carneades transmitted through Clitomachus, NOT to Antiochus of Ascalon (the standard alternative). The doxographical attribution rests on Cicero's reading of Magna Moralia 1187b29 ('phusis is needed for a man to be good') as making external/natural endowments rather than the autonomous soul the cause of moral action. THIS ENTIRE CHAPTER WAS EXCLUDED FROM THE 2010 PEETERS VOLUME by Donini's own decision (Prefatory Note: 'The sixth and final chapter of the Italian edition of the book has instead been omitted, as it was less important than the essays, both from a strictly philosophical point of view, and in relation to modern discussions of Aristotle's position on the question of determinism.'). Therefore the thesis CANNOT be verified verbatim from the 2010 volume on disk; only Huby's 1991 review attests it.
scholarly_argument_donini_cicero_s_de_fa.primary_attestation: Huby 1991 review p.370-371 (paraphrase of Donini 1989 Ch. VI)
scholarly_argument_donini_cicero_s_de_fa.explicitly_not_in_2010_volume: Donini himself omitted Ch. VI of Ethos 1989 from the 2010 Peeters volume — Prefatory Note p.v
scholarly_argument_donini_cicero_s_de_fa.not_in_local_corpus: Donini, Ethos: Aristotele e il determinismo, Alessandria: Edizioni dell'Orso, 1989, Ch. VI (esp. pp. ca. 137-154) — physical monograph required for direct verification of the Carneades/Clitomachus thesis
